Original vs. Revised Composite Threshold ComparisonÂ¶

The composite score calculation remains unchanged. The only change is the regime threshold framework used to classify the score into Normal, Watch, Elevated, or Stress.

The original thresholds used 50 / 75 / 90, which worked for individual percentile-style category scores but proved too conservative for the equal-weighted composite score. The revised thresholds use 45 / 55 / 70 to better reflect the observed historical distribution of the composite score.

This comparison shows the same composite score under both threshold frameworks.

InÂ [56]:
threshold_comparison_summary = pd.read_sql_query(
    """
    SELECT
        threshold_version,
        regime,
        month_count
    FROM (
        SELECT
            'Original thresholds: 50 / 75 / 90' AS threshold_version,
            composite_credit_risk_regime AS regime,
            COUNT(*) AS month_count,
            1 AS threshold_sort,
            CASE composite_credit_risk_regime
                WHEN 'Normal' THEN 1
                WHEN 'Watch' THEN 2
                WHEN 'Elevated' THEN 3
                WHEN 'Stress' THEN 4
                ELSE 5
            END AS regime_sort
        FROM credit_risk_composite_scores_revised
        WHERE composite_score_coverage_pct = 100
        GROUP BY composite_credit_risk_regime

        UNION ALL

        SELECT
            'Revised thresholds: 45 / 55 / 70' AS threshold_version,
            composite_credit_risk_regime_revised AS regime,
            COUNT(*) AS month_count,
            2 AS threshold_sort,
            CASE composite_credit_risk_regime_revised
                WHEN 'Normal' THEN 1
                WHEN 'Watch' THEN 2
                WHEN 'Elevated' THEN 3
                WHEN 'Stress' THEN 4
                ELSE 5
            END AS regime_sort
        FROM credit_risk_composite_scores_revised
        WHERE composite_score_coverage_pct = 100
        GROUP BY composite_credit_risk_regime_revised
    )
    ORDER BY threshold_sort, regime_sort;
    """,
    conn
)

  • Normal: Broad credit-risk conditions are within the lower historical range of the composite score. Individual categories may still show pressure, but the overall system-level score is not elevated.

  • Watch: Conditions are above normal and deserve monitoring. A Watch regime does not imply crisis; it means the composite score has moved into a range where one or more categories are showing meaningful deterioration.

  • Elevated: Conditions are materially stressed and closer to recession-like behavior. Elevated months indicate that risk is broadening across categories or that one or more categories have become severe enough to raise the composite score.

  • Stress: Conditions resemble the most severe historical macro-credit stress periods in the available sample. Stress is reserved for broad-based deterioration across multiple categories, not just a single market shock.

Threshold Selection RationaleÂ¶

The revised composite thresholds were selected after validating the original regime framework against recession and non-recession months. The original 50 / 75 / 90 thresholds were appropriate as an initial percentile-style framework, but they were too conservative for the equal-weighted composite score. Because the composite score averages four category scores, extreme values in one category are dampened by lower values in other categories.

The revised thresholds are:

  • Below 45: Normal
  • 45 to below 55: Watch
  • 55 to below 70: Elevated
  • 70 and above: Stress

These thresholds are calibrated to the observed composite-score behavior. The non-recession average score is approximately 42.7, so 45 marks the transition from normal conditions to above-normal monitoring pressure. The minimum recession-month score is approximately 53.9, so 55 marks the beginning of recession-like deterioration risk. The average recession-month score is approximately 69.8, and the non-recession maximum is approximately 67.1, so 70 is used as the Stress threshold to reserve the highest-risk label for historically severe broad-based credit stress.

The thresholds are not regulatory cutoffs and should not be interpreted as causal recession predictors. They are transparent monitoring thresholds designed to translate the composite score into usable dashboard regimes. Category-level scores remain available to explain whether the composite score is being driven by market stress, labor deterioration, rate/yield-curve pressure, or realized credit performance.

Threshold Sensitivity and TradeoffÂ¶

The revised thresholds are intended to classify the composite score as a macro-credit monitoring signal, not as a pure market-stress alarm. Lowering the Stress threshold too aggressively would make the dashboard more sensitive to sudden market shocks, but it would also increase the risk of false stress classifications during non-recession or temporary volatility periods.

The selected 45 / 55 / 70 framework balances sensitivity and conservatism. A Watch threshold of 45 is slightly above the average non-recession composite score, so it identifies above-normal pressure without labeling ordinary conditions as risky. An Elevated threshold of 55 is near the lower bound of observed recession-month composite scores, so it captures recession-like deterioration. A Stress threshold of 70 is near the average recession-month composite score and above the observed non-recession maximum, so it reserves the highest-risk label for broad-based macro-credit stress rather than isolated market volatility.

A lower Stress threshold, such as 60 or 65, would capture more abrupt shock periods, including parts of the COVID episode. However, that would shift the model closer to a market-stress detector. Realized credit performance did not deteriorate during the COVID period in the same way as it did during 2008. Policy intervention, payment forbearance, stimulus, and the short recession length muted the realized credit-loss channel. Therefore, if COVID does not reach the composite Stress regime, that is not necessarily a model failure. It means the model is distinguishing between a market shock / labor shock and a full macro-credit deterioration cycle.

The 70 threshold is retained because the dashboard is designed to identify broad macro-credit deterioration across market stress, labor risk, rate pressure, and realized credit performance.

Revised Regime vs. Recession Validation InterpretationÂ¶

The revised regime framework produces economically sensible separation across recession and non-recession months. Normal months contain no recession observations, and Watch months contain only a very small recession share. Elevated months contain a much higher recession share, indicating that the revised Elevated regime captures meaningful macro-credit deterioration.

The Stress regime contains only recession months in this historical sample. This supports the decision to use 70 as the revised Stress threshold because it reserves the highest-risk label for severe broad-based macro-credit stress rather than temporary or isolated market volatility.

This validation does not prove forecasting power because the recession indicator is used as a historical classification label, not as a future outcome. However, it confirms that the revised regime labels align more closely with known recession periods than the original thresholds. The result supports using the revised regime framework for dashboard interpretation.

The next validation step is to test whether revised regime labels provide useful forward-looking market context by comparing future S&P 500 returns across Normal, Watch, Elevated, and Stress regimes.

revised_recession_regime_check = pd.read_sql_query(
    """
    SELECT
        composite_credit_risk_regime_revised AS revised_regime,
        COUNT(*) AS month_count,

        SUM(
            CASE
                WHEN usrec = 1 THEN 1
                ELSE 0
            END
        ) AS recession_months,

        ROUND(
            100.0 * SUM(
                CASE
                    WHEN usrec = 1 THEN 1
                    ELSE 0
                END
            ) / COUNT(*),
            2
        ) AS recession_share_pct,

        AVG(composite_credit_risk_score) AS avg_score,
        MIN(composite_credit_risk_score) AS min_score,
        MAX(composite_credit_risk_score) AS max_score

    FROM credit_risk_composite_scores_revised
    WHERE composite_score_coverage_pct = 100
    GROUP BY composite_credit_risk_regime_revised
    ORDER BY
        CASE composite_credit_risk_regime_revised
            WHEN 'Normal' THEN 1
            WHEN 'Watch' THEN 2
            WHEN 'Elevated' THEN 3
            WHEN 'Stress' THEN 4
            ELSE 5
        END;
    """,
    conn
)

7.7.2 Forward S&P 500 Return ValidationÂ¶

The recession validation tested whether the revised composite regimes aligned with known macroeconomic stress periods. This next check evaluates the market-context overlay by comparing future S&P 500 returns across the revised risk regimes.

The question is:

When the dashboard classified conditions as Normal, Watch, or Elevated, did future S&P 500 returns show different return patterns?

This is not a trading rule and does not prove causality. The purpose is to test whether the macro-credit regime contains useful forward-looking market context. If forward S&P 500 returns differ across risk regimes, then the dashboard may have practical value for risk-on / risk-off interpretation, portfolio monitoring, and market-context discussion.

The S&P 500 overlay begins later than the full credit-risk dataset because the FRED S&P 500 series used in this project starts in 2016. Therefore, this validation only uses months where forward S&P 500 return data are available. Some regimes, especially Stress, may have limited or no observations in the S&P 500 overlay window.

This table compares future S&P 500 returns across the revised composite risk regimes. The goal is to determine whether higher dashboard risk regimes were historically associated with different forward equity-market outcomes in the available S&P 500 market-context window.

The result should be interpreted carefully because the S&P 500 overlay begins in 2016, while the full credit-risk score begins earlier. As a result, the forward-return validation has fewer observations than the recession validation and may not include all historical stress periods.

The key evaluation question is whether average forward returns, positive-return shares, and downside outcomes differ as the regime moves from Normal to Watch to Elevated.

    SELECT
        composite_credit_risk_regime_revised AS revised_regime,

        COUNT(*) AS month_count,

        ROUND(100.0 * AVG(sp500_forward_1m_return), 2) AS avg_forward_1m_return_pct,

Forward S&P 500 Return Validation InterpretationÂ¶

This validation evaluates whether the revised macro-credit risk regimes provide useful forward-looking context for S&P 500 returns. This section is not part of the core credit-risk score. It is a market-context validation layer that tests whether the dashboardâ€™s macro-credit regimes are associated with different future equity-return profiles.

The analysis is a state-conditioned return check. For every month classified as Normal, Watch, or Elevated, the table calculates the following forward S&P 500 outcomes:

  • average next 1-month return
  • average next 3-month return
  • average next 6-month return
  • share of observations with positive forward returns
  • minimum and maximum observed 3-month forward returns

This answers the question:

When the dashboard classified the current month as a specific macro-credit regime, what happened to S&P 500 returns afterward?

The results show that the relationship between macro-credit stress and forward equity returns is not one-directional in the available S&P 500 market-context window. Elevated months had stronger average forward returns than Normal or Watch months, and Elevated months also had higher positive-return shares across the 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month forward windows.

This result suggests that elevated macro-credit stress can coincide with rebound conditions rather than only downside conditions. One possible explanation is timing. By the time the dashboard reaches an Elevated regime, markets may have already repriced bad news. Equity markets may then begin responding to stabilization, liquidity support, policy response, improved risk appetite, or expectations that conditions will stop deteriorating.

This does not mean that elevated credit risk is bullish by itself. It means that the composite score measures macro-credit stress, not the full set of variables that determine equity returns. The current composite includes market stress, labor risk, rate/yield-curve pressure, and realized credit performance. It does not include all drivers of equity returns, such as inflation, Federal Reserve policy, bank lending standards, corporate earnings expectations, equity valuation, liquidity conditions, or investor positioning.

Because of that, the correct interpretation is narrower: the dashboard provides macro-credit regime context, and the S&P 500 overlay tests whether those regimes are associated with different forward equity outcomes. The result shows that the score is useful for framing market conditions, but the state-conditioned regime level alone should not be treated as a mechanical equity-return forecast.

The next check evaluates regime transitions directly. That matters because the current table groups together all months inside a regime, including months where the regime just changed, months where the regime persisted, and months where stress may already have started to fade. A transition-based check can test whether moves such as Normal to Watch or Watch to Elevated carry different information than the regime level alone.

Monetary Policy and Macro Variable LimitationÂ¶

This first-version composite score includes rate pressure through the 30-year Treasury yield, the 30-year Treasury 3-month change, and yield-curve inversion risk. However, it does not directly include the Federal Funds rate, CPI inflation, core CPI inflation, real interest rates, bank loan demand, bank lending standards, corporate earnings expectations, equity valuation, or investor positioning.

These omitted variables matter for a broader macro-credit monitoring framework. For example, CPI inflation and Federal Reserve policy affect discount rates, borrowing costs, credit conditions, and market liquidity. Bank lending standards and loan demand provide direct information about credit availability. The Federal Reserveâ€™s Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey is a potential source for lending-standard and loan-demand indicators.

These variables are not added to the first version because the project is designed as a transparent macro-credit monitoring dashboard. Version 1 prioritizes reproducibility, interpretability, and a clear scoring framework before adding additional macro-policy and lending-channel complexity.

Future versions could add Federal Funds rate, CPI inflation, core CPI inflation, real interest rates, SLOOS lending standards, SLOOS loan demand, and credit-to-GDP measures to improve policy, inflation, and lending-channel coverage.

7.7.2b Regime Transition Return CheckÂ¶

The prior validation measured forward returns based on the current regime level. This transition check asks a different question: did forward S&P 500 returns differ after the dashboard changed from one regime to another?

Examples include:

  • Normal â†’ Watch
  • Watch â†’ Elevated
  • Elevated â†’ Watch
  • Watch â†’ Normal

This is closer to an event-study style check. Instead of asking what happened after all Elevated months, it asks what happened after the dashboard first moved into a different state. This can help identify whether regime changes contain incremental information beyond the regime level alone.

This distinction matters because the state-conditioned table mixes several situations together:

  • months where a regime just changed
  • months where the same regime persisted
  • months where stress was already fading
  • months where markets may have already started recovering

The transition table separates those cases more directly. However, transition counts may be small, so the results should be interpreted as exploratory evidence rather than a standalone trading rule.

InÂ [60]:
transition_event_data = pd.read_sql_query(
    """
    WITH regime_history AS (
        SELECT
            month_end,

            composite_credit_risk_score AS current_score,

            LAG(composite_credit_risk_score)
                OVER (ORDER BY month_end) AS prior_score,

            composite_credit_risk_regime_revised AS current_regime,

            LAG(composite_credit_risk_regime_revised)
                OVER (ORDER BY month_end) AS prior_regime,

            usrec,

            sp500_forward_1m_return,
            sp500_forward_3m_return,
            sp500_forward_6m_return

        FROM credit_risk_composite_scores_revised
        WHERE composite_score_coverage_pct = 100
          AND sp500_forward_1m_return IS NOT NULL
          AND sp500_forward_3m_return IS NOT NULL
          AND sp500_forward_6m_return IS NOT NULL
    )

    SELECT
        month_end,
        prior_regime || ' -> ' || current_regime AS regime_transition,
        prior_regime,
        current_regime,
        prior_score,
        current_score,
        current_score - prior_score AS score_change,
        usrec,
        sp500_forward_1m_return,
        sp500_forward_3m_return,
        sp500_forward_6m_return

    FROM regime_history
    WHERE prior_regime IS NOT NULL
      AND prior_regime <> current_regime

    ORDER BY month_end;
    """,
    conn
)

transition_event_data["month_end"] = pd.to_datetime(
    transition_event_data["month_end"]
)

transition_summary_rows = []

for transition, subset in transition_event_data.groupby("regime_transition"):
    transition_count = len(subset)

    if transition_count >= 30:
        sample_strength = "Stronger sample"
    elif transition_count >= 10:
        sample_strength = "Limited sample"
    elif transition_count >= 5:
        sample_strength = "Very limited sample"
    else:
        sample_strength = "Anecdotal sample"

    transition_summary_rows.append({
        "regime_transition": transition,
        "transition_count": transition_count,
        "sample_strength": sample_strength,

        "avg_score_change": subset["score_change"].mean(),
        "recession_share_pct": subset["usrec"].mean() * 100,

        "avg_forward_1m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_1m_return"].mean() * 100,
        "avg_forward_3m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"].mean() * 100,
        "avg_forward_6m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_6m_return"].mean() * 100,

        "median_forward_3m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"].median() * 100,

        "negative_1m_return_share_pct": (subset["sp500_forward_1m_return"] < 0).mean() * 100,
        "negative_3m_return_share_pct": (subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"] < 0).mean() * 100,
        "negative_6m_return_share_pct": (subset["sp500_forward_6m_return"] < 0).mean() * 100,

        "worst_forward_3m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"].min() * 100
    })

regime_transition_return_check_final = pd.DataFrame(
    transition_summary_rows
)

regime_transition_return_check_final = (
    regime_transition_return_check_final
    .sort_values("transition_count", ascending=False)
    .round(2)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

Regime Transition Metric DefinitionsÂ¶

This table evaluates what happened after the dashboard moved from one revised macro-credit regime to another. It does not calculate a correlation coefficient. Instead, it is a transition-conditioned forward return analysis: for each month where the regime changed, the table summarizes the Composite Credit Risk Score movement and the subsequent S&P 500 forward returns.

The transition_count column shows how many times each regime transition occurred in the available S&P 500 forward-return window. For example, a Normal â†’ Watch transition means the prior month was classified as Normal and the current month moved into Watch.

The avg_score_change column measures the average change in the Composite Credit Risk Score during the transition month. This is measured in score points on the 0-to-100 composite-risk scale. For example, an average score change of 6.48 means the composite score increased by about 6.48 points when that transition occurred.

The recession_share_pct column shows the percentage of transition months that occurred during an NBER recession month.

The avg_forward_1m_return_pct, avg_forward_3m_return_pct, and avg_forward_6m_return_pct columns measure the average S&P 500 return after the transition month over the next 1, 3, and 6 months. These are forward market outcomes, not changes in the credit-risk score.

The negative-return share columns measure downside frequency, not downside severity. For example, a negative 1-month return share of 40% means that 40% of the transition observations had a negative 1-month forward S&P 500 return. It does not show how large those negative returns were.

For the 3-month and 6-month negative-return share columns, the calculation checks whether the full cumulative forward return over that horizon was negative. It does not count whether any single month inside the forward window was negative.

The median_forward_3m_return_pct column reports the middle 3-month forward S&P 500 return after each transition. The 3-month median is included as a practical medium-term monitoring measure because it is less noisy than the 1-month return and less extended than the 6-month return.

The worst_forward_3m_return_pct column reports the worst observed cumulative 3-month S&P 500 return after each transition. This gives one downside-severity measure at the transition level. Negative-return share shows how often downside occurred, while worst forward return shows the largest observed downside event in that horizon.

This transition table should be interpreted as exploratory market-context evidence. It is useful for identifying possible monitoring signals, but several transition groups have small sample sizes, so the results should not be treated as statistically conclusive.

Regime Transition Return Check InterpretationÂ¶

This transition check evaluates whether changes in the revised macro-credit regime contain additional information beyond the regime level alone. Instead of grouping every month by its current regime, this table focuses only on months where the dashboard changed from one regime to another.

The table is intentionally focused on practical risk-monitoring metrics: transition count, average composite score change, recession share, average forward S&P 500 returns, negative-return shares, and worst observed 3-month forward return. Standard deviation is excluded from the final display because several transition groups contain very few observations, making dispersion statistics less stable and harder to interpret.

The clearest warning transition is Normal â†’ Watch. This transition occurred 10 times and had an average composite score increase of 6.48 points on the 0-to-100 score scale. The average forward S&P 500 returns were still positive at 0.44% over 1 month, 3.30% over 3 months, and 6.27% over 6 months. However, this transition also had the worst observed 3-month forward S&P 500 return at -16.45%, along with negative-return shares of 40.0% over 1 month, 20.0% over 3 months, and 30.0% over 6 months. This suggests that the first move out of Normal conditions is the most useful transition warning in the current results.

The Watch â†’ Elevated transition occurred 4 times and had an average composite score increase of 7.10 points. It also had a 25.0% recession-month share. Forward S&P 500 returns were strong in this small sample, averaging 4.37% over 1 month, 12.02% over 3 months, and 16.21% over 6 months. The worst observed 3-month forward return was still positive at 9.66%. This result should not be overinterpreted because the sample is small. It suggests that some transitions into Elevated may occur after market stress has already been priced in, with forward returns improving as conditions stabilize or policy/liquidity support becomes more visible.

The Watch â†’ Normal transition occurred 8 times and represents improving dashboard conditions. It had an average composite score decline of -8.15 points, no recession-month observations, and positive average forward returns of 3.04% over 3 months and 5.35% over 6 months. The worst 3-month forward return was only -1.16%, which is directionally consistent with lower downside pressure after conditions improve.

The Elevated â†’ Watch transition occurred 3 times and had an average composite score decline of -7.44 points. Forward returns were positive across all horizons, averaging 3.35% over 1 month, 8.80% over 3 months, and 13.39% over 6 months. This is consistent with recovery or de-escalation behavior, but the sample is anecdotal because only three transition events are available.

The Elevated â†’ Normal transition has only one observation and should not be used for inference. It is included for transparency, but the sample size is too small to interpret as a recurring pattern.

Overall, the transition results support using the dashboard as a macro-credit monitoring tool with market-context validation. The transition analysis shows that Normal â†’ Watch is the clearest early-warning move because it had the worst observed 3-month downside and the highest short-window negative-return frequency. Watch â†’ Elevated and de-escalation transitions showed positive average forward returns in this sample, which suggests that the S&P 500 relationship is timing-dependent and not mechanically bearish.

The correct conclusion is not that regime transitions reliably predict S&P 500 returns. The correct conclusion is that regime transitions provide market-context information. They can help frame whether conditions are moving into a more fragile macro-credit state, but they should not be treated as standalone trading rules.

7.7.3 Forward Return Downside ValidationÂ¶

The previous checks evaluated average forward S&P 500 returns by regime level and by regime transition. This section focuses more directly on downside risk.

Average returns can hide important information. A regime may have a positive average return while still containing larger downside events, higher negative-return frequency, or wider risk exposure. For a macro-credit monitoring dashboard, the more relevant question is not only whether forward returns were positive or negative on average, but whether higher-risk regimes were associated with greater downside risk.

This validation compares forward S&P 500 downside behavior across revised composite regimes using:

  • month count
  • recession share
  • average forward returns
  • median forward returns
  • negative-return shares
  • worst observed forward returns

This section helps determine whether the composite regime provides useful risk-context information even when average forward returns are positive.

InÂ [61]:
forward_downside_data = pd.read_sql_query(
    """
    SELECT
        month_end,
        composite_credit_risk_regime_revised AS revised_regime,
        composite_credit_risk_score,
        usrec,
        sp500_forward_1m_return,
        sp500_forward_3m_return,
        sp500_forward_6m_return
    FROM credit_risk_composite_scores_revised
    WHERE composite_score_coverage_pct = 100
      AND sp500_forward_1m_return IS NOT NULL
      AND sp500_forward_3m_return IS NOT NULL
      AND sp500_forward_6m_return IS NOT NULL
    ORDER BY month_end;
    """,
    conn
)

forward_downside_data["month_end"] = pd.to_datetime(
    forward_downside_data["month_end"]
)

regime_order = ["Normal", "Watch", "Elevated", "Stress"]

downside_summary_rows = []

for regime in regime_order:
    subset = forward_downside_data[
        forward_downside_data["revised_regime"] == regime
    ]

    month_count = len(subset)

    if month_count == 0:
        continue

    if month_count >= 30:
        sample_strength = "Stronger sample"
    elif month_count >= 10:
        sample_strength = "Limited sample"
    elif month_count >= 5:
        sample_strength = "Very limited sample"
    else:
        sample_strength = "Anecdotal sample"

    downside_summary_rows.append({
        "revised_regime": regime,
        "month_count": month_count,
        "sample_strength": sample_strength,

        "avg_composite_score": subset["composite_credit_risk_score"].mean(),
        "recession_share_pct": subset["usrec"].mean() * 100,

        "avg_forward_1m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_1m_return"].mean() * 100,
        "avg_forward_3m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"].mean() * 100,
        "avg_forward_6m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_6m_return"].mean() * 100,

        "median_forward_1m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_1m_return"].median() * 100,
        "median_forward_3m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"].median() * 100,
        "median_forward_6m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_6m_return"].median() * 100,

        "negative_1m_return_share_pct": (subset["sp500_forward_1m_return"] < 0).mean() * 100,
        "negative_3m_return_share_pct": (subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"] < 0).mean() * 100,
        "negative_6m_return_share_pct": (subset["sp500_forward_6m_return"] < 0).mean() * 100,

        "worst_forward_1m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_1m_return"].min() * 100,
        "worst_forward_3m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_3m_return"].min() * 100,
        "worst_forward_6m_return_pct": subset["sp500_forward_6m_return"].min() * 100
    })

forward_return_downside_validation = pd.DataFrame(
    downside_summary_rows
)

forward_return_downside_validation = (
    forward_return_downside_validation
    .round(2)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

Forward Return Downside Validation InterpretationÂ¶

This downside validation evaluates whether higher revised macro-credit regimes were associated with weaker or riskier forward S&P 500 outcomes. The goal is not only to compare average returns, but also to examine downside frequency and worst observed forward returns.

The results show clearer separation for macro stress than for equity downside. Recession share rises across the regimes: Normal has a 0.00% recession share, Watch has a 2.44% recession share, and Elevated has a 12.50% recession share. This supports the interpretation that higher composite regimes are associated with greater macro-credit stress.

However, the forward equity-return results do not show a simple pattern where higher regimes have worse S&P 500 downside. Normal months had an average 6-month forward return of 5.15%, Watch months had an average 6-month forward return of 7.23%, and Elevated months had an average 6-month forward return of 17.95%. Elevated months also had no negative 3-month or 6-month forward returns in this sample.

The downside metrics show a similar pattern. Normal had the worst observed 3-month forward return at -20.00%, while Watch had a worst observed 3-month forward return of -16.45%. Elevated had a positive worst observed 3-month forward return of 8.47%. This suggests that the Elevated regime in the available S&P 500 overlay window was more associated with stress-and-rebound behavior than with continued forward downside.

The Watch regime provides the more useful caution signal. Watch months had a higher average composite score than Normal months, a higher recession share, and a slightly higher negative 1-month return share. This suggests that Watch may capture early deterioration or unstable conditions, even though average forward returns remained positive.

The Elevated result should be interpreted carefully because it contains only 8 observations, making it a very limited sample. The absence of negative 3-month or 6-month returns in Elevated does not prove that Elevated conditions are low risk. It indicates that, in the available overlay window, Elevated observations often occurred after market stress had already been reflected in prices and forward returns improved afterward.

Overall, this validation supports the dashboard as a macro-credit monitoring framework with useful market-context information. The composite regime is effective for identifying rising macro-credit stress, but the S&P 500 overlay does not support treating higher regimes as automatic equity downside signals. The equity interpretation is more nuanced: elevated macro-credit stress can coincide with market drawdowns, but it can also appear near rebound periods after conditions have already deteriorated.

7.7.4 Final Threshold Validation ConclusionÂ¶

The threshold validation supports using the revised 45 / 55 / 70 composite regime framework for the first version of the dashboard.

The original 50 / 75 / 90 thresholds were useful as an initial percentile-style structure, but they were too conservative for an equal-weighted composite score. Because the composite averages four category scores, extreme values in one category can be dampened by lower values in other categories. As a result, the original framework produced no Stress months, even during major historical stress periods.

The revised thresholds create a more practical regime structure:

  • Normal: below 45
  • Watch: 45 to below 55
  • Elevated: 55 to below 70
  • Stress: 70 and above

The recession validation provides the strongest support for the revised thresholds. Normal months had a 0.00% recession share, Watch months had a low recession share, Elevated months had a materially higher recession share, and Stress months were concentrated in recession periods. This indicates that the revised regimes create economically sensible separation across known macroeconomic stress periods.

The S&P 500 overlay provides additional market-context validation, but the results are more nuanced. State-conditioned and transition-based return checks show that higher macro-credit regimes do not mechanically translate into weaker future S&P 500 returns. In several cases, Elevated regimes were followed by strong forward returns, likely because markets had already repriced stress or were beginning to respond to stabilization, policy support, liquidity improvement, or recovering risk appetite.

This distinction is important for interpreting the dashboard correctly. The composite score is not a standalone equity-market forecasting model. It is a macro-credit risk monitoring framework with a light S&P 500 overlay. The primary purpose is to evaluate whether macro-credit conditions are deteriorating, stabilizing, or improving. The equity overlay helps provide context for market behavior around those regimes, but it should not be treated as a mechanical buy/sell signal.

Overall, the revised threshold framework is retained because it improves regime classification, aligns better with recession-period stress, and supports clearer dashboard interpretation. The final Version 1 model should be positioned as a transparent macro-credit monitoring dashboard that summarizes market stress, labor risk, rate/yield-curve pressure, and realized credit performance into an interpretable composite regime score.

7.8 Section 6â€“7 Implementation RecapÂ¶

Sections 6 and 7 converted the cleaned monthly macro-credit dataset into a structured credit-risk monitoring framework. The main objective was to transform raw economic and financial indicators into comparable risk signals, aggregate them into category scores, construct a composite credit-risk score, and validate whether the resulting regimes behaved sensibly during known stress periods.

The first question was: how should different indicators be made comparable?
The project solved this by converting raw variables into directional risk features where higher values consistently represent higher risk. For example, higher VIX, financial stress, unemployment, credit spreads, delinquency rates, and charge-off rates already represent higher risk. The yield-curve feature was transformed so that inversion pressure also maps to higher risk.

The second question was: how should the score avoid lookahead bias?
The project created expanding percentile features rather than relying only on full-sample retrospective percentiles. Retrospective percentiles are useful for historical visualization, but expanding percentiles are more appropriate for monitoring because each month is compared only against information available up to that point. A 60-month warm-up window was used before operational expanding-percentile scoring begins.

The third question was: how should indicators be grouped?
The model groups indicators into four risk categories:

  • Market / Financial Stress
  • Macro / Labor Risk
  • Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure
  • Realized Credit Performance

These categories allow the dashboard to show both the overall composite score and the underlying drivers of that score. This is important because two months can have the same composite score but very different risk compositions.

The fourth question was: how should the composite score be calculated?
The composite score is calculated as an equal-weighted average of the four category scores. This creates a transparent score from 0 to 100, where higher values indicate more severe macro-credit stress. The equal-weighted structure was chosen for interpretability and to avoid overfitting a small number of historical stress episodes.

The fifth question was: what thresholds should define Normal, Watch, Elevated, and Stress regimes?
The original 50 / 75 / 90 threshold framework was useful as an initial percentile-style structure, but it was too conservative for an equal-weighted composite score. Because the composite averages four category scores, extreme values in one category can be dampened by lower values in other categories. The original framework produced no Stress months, even during major historical stress periods.

The revised thresholds were set to:

  • Normal: below 45
  • Watch: 45 to below 55
  • Elevated: 55 to below 70
  • Stress: 70 and above

The revised thresholds produced a more practical regime distribution: 141 Normal months, 78 Watch months, 31 Elevated months, and 9 Stress months among fully scored observations.

The sixth question was: did the revised regimes align with known recession periods?
The recession validation supported the revised framework. Normal months had a 0.00% recession share, Watch months had a 1.28% recession share, Elevated months had a 32.26% recession share, and Stress months had a 100.00% recession share in the scored sample. This indicates that the revised thresholds create stronger economic separation across known stress periods.

The seventh question was: did the S&P 500 overlay show a simple relationship between higher credit-risk regimes and weaker forward equity returns?
The answer was no. In the available S&P 500 overlay window, Elevated months had stronger average forward returns than Normal or Watch months. This suggests that the composite score should not be interpreted as a direct equity-market sell signal. Instead, the equity overlay provides market-context evidence around macro-credit regimes.

The eighth question was: did regime transitions provide useful market context?
The transition analysis showed that the Normal to Watch transition was the clearest early-warning move. It occurred 10 times, had an average composite score increase of 6.48 points, and contained the worst observed 3-month forward S&P 500 return at -16.45%. However, transition counts were limited, so these results are best interpreted as diagnostic context rather than a mechanical trading rule.

Several implementation issues were also identified and addressed. Early missing values were expected because 3-month changes require lagged observations. Expanding percentile scores required a warm-up period before becoming operational. Forward S&P 500 returns were unavailable before the FRED S&P 500 series begins and unavailable at the end of the sample where future returns are not yet known. These missing values were not treated as data errors; they were documented as structural limitations of the feature and validation design.

Overall, Sections 6 and 7 establish the core framework of the project. The dashboard now has a reproducible pipeline that transforms public macro-credit indicators into category scores, combines them into a composite credit-risk score, assigns interpretable regimes, and validates those regimes against recession periods and S&P 500 forward-return behavior. The resulting model is best positioned as a macro-credit risk monitoring dashboard with a light S&P 500 overlay.

8. Credit Risk ScoreÂ¶

Section 8 converts the revised scoring framework into the final dashboard-ready credit-risk score output. The goal is to summarize the latest composite score, latest regime, category-level drivers, recent score momentum, and a simple forward risk outlook.

The forward outlook in this section is not a stock-price forecast. It is a baseline credit-risk score projection based on recent composite-score momentum. The purpose is to determine whether macro-credit conditions are currently improving, stabilizing, or deteriorating over the next 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month monitoring windows.

8.1 Final Credit Risk Score TableÂ¶

The final credit-risk score table combines the revised composite score, revised regime label, four category-level risk scores, recession indicator, score coverage, provisional flag, and recent score changes.

Each category score is measured on a 0 to 100 scale. A higher value means that category is showing higher historical risk pressure relative to its own expanding historical distribution. These category scores are not regression coefficients. They are percentile-based risk scores designed to make indicators with different units comparable.

The four category scores are:

  • Market / Financial Stress Score: captures market volatility, financial stress, and credit-spread pressure.
  • Macro / Labor Risk Score: captures labor-market deterioration, mainly through unemployment-related features.
  • Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure Score: captures interest-rate pressure and yield-curve inversion risk.
  • Realized Credit Performance Score: captures observed credit deterioration through delinquency and charge-off indicators.

The composite score is calculated as the equal-weighted average of the four category scores. Because each category contributes one-fourth of the final score, the composite score summarizes broad macro-credit stress while still allowing the dashboard to identify which category is driving the current reading.

The composite_score_coverage_pct field shows whether all category scores are available for that month. A value of 100 means the composite score is fully covered. The provisional_composite_flag identifies months where the score should be interpreted cautiously because of warm-up periods, missing feature history, or incomplete scoring inputs.

The 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month score changes are point-to-point changes in the composite score, not rolling averages. For example, the 3-month change equals the current composite score minus the composite score from three months earlier.

The provisional_composite_flag identifies months where the Composite Credit Risk Score should be interpreted cautiously. A provisional score may occur during early calibration periods or when one or more expected category inputs are unavailable. The score is still calculated using the available category information, but the flag separates fully covered operational scores from scores that depend on partial information.

8.2 Current Credit Risk Snapshot and Category DriversÂ¶

This section summarizes the latest dashboard reading and identifies which components are driving the current credit-risk score. It combines the current composite score, current regime, recent score changes, and category-level drivers into one dashboard-ready snapshot.

This section answers two current-state monitoring questions:

Are macro-credit conditions currently improving, stabilizing, or deteriorating?

Which part of the credit-risk environment is contributing most to the current score?

The composite score is the equal-weighted average of the four category scores. Each category score is measured on a 0 to 100 scale, where higher values indicate greater historical risk pressure in that category.

The score-change columns are point-to-point changes, not rolling averages:

  • 1-month change: current score minus the score from one month earlier
  • 3-month change: current score minus the score from three months earlier
  • 6-month change: current score minus the score from six months earlier

A positive change means risk pressure increased over that lookback window. A negative change means risk pressure declined. A stable reading means the score changed by less than one point.

This structure allows the dashboard to separate the overall risk level from the underlying drivers. For example, the composite score may be Normal, while one individual category may still be elevated. That distinction is important because it shows whether risk is broad-based across the system or concentrated in one part of the macro-credit environment.

8.3 Forward Credit Risk OutlookÂ¶

This section creates a forward credit-risk outlook for the composite score and each category score. The purpose is to estimate whether macro-credit pressure is likely to improve, stabilize, or deteriorate over the next 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month monitoring windows.

The forecast is applied to the dashboardâ€™s own risk scores, not to S&P 500 prices. The goal is to project the composite score and the four category scores forward so the dashboard can provide a short-term macro-credit risk outlook.

A simple time-series baseline is used for this first version of the dashboard. Rather than assuming one fixed structure for every score component, candidate ARIMA models can be compared using AIC and BIC. This is important because different score components may behave differently. Market stress may mean-revert quickly, while labor risk and realized credit performance may move more slowly and persistently.

The forecast should be interpreted as a monitoring outlook, not a guaranteed prediction. The purpose is to show whether the current score path points toward improving, stable, or deteriorating conditions and whether projected scores remain comfortably within the current regime or approach a higher-risk threshold.

InÂ [64]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

def assign_composite_regime(score):
    if pd.isna(score):
        return "Insufficient Data"
    elif score < 45:
        return "Normal"
    elif score < 55:
        return "Watch"
    elif score < 70:
        return "Elevated"
    else:
        return "Stress"


def assign_category_band(score):
    if pd.isna(score):
        return "Insufficient Data"
    elif score < 50:
        return "Normal"
    elif score < 75:
        return "Watch"
    elif score < 90:
        return "Elevated"
    else:
        return "Stress"


score_columns = {
    "Composite Credit Risk Score": "composite_credit_risk_score",
    "Market / Financial Stress": "market_financial_stress_score",
    "Macro / Labor Risk": "macro_labor_risk_score",
    "Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure": "rate_yield_curve_pressure_score",
    "Realized Credit Performance": "realized_credit_performance_score"
}

forecast_horizons = {
    "Current": 0,
    "Projected 1-month": 1,
    "Projected 3-month": 3,
    "Projected 6-month": 6
}

forward_outlook_rows = []
forecast_model_diagnostics = []

for component_name, score_col in score_columns.items():
    model_data = dashboard_score_data[
        ["month_end", score_col]
    ].dropna().copy()

    model_data["lag_score"] = model_data[score_col].shift(1)
    model_data = model_data.dropna()

    y = model_data[score_col]
    X = sm.add_constant(model_data["lag_score"])

    ar1_model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()

    intercept = ar1_model.params["const"]
    beta = ar1_model.params["lag_score"]
    residual_std = ar1_model.resid.std()

    latest_score = dashboard_score_data[score_col].iloc[-1]

    recursive_forecasts = {
        "Current": latest_score
    }

    forecast_score = latest_score

    for step in range(1, 7):
        forecast_score = intercept + beta * forecast_score
        forecast_score = min(max(forecast_score, 0), 100)

        if step == 1:
            recursive_forecasts["Projected 1-month"] = forecast_score
        elif step == 3:
            recursive_forecasts["Projected 3-month"] = forecast_score
        elif step == 6:
            recursive_forecasts["Projected 6-month"] = forecast_score

    for outlook_window, projected_score in recursive_forecasts.items():
        if component_name == "Composite Credit Risk Score":
            projected_classification = assign_composite_regime(projected_score)
        else:
            projected_classification = assign_category_band(projected_score)

        forward_outlook_rows.append({
            "score_component": component_name,
            "outlook_window": outlook_window,
            "projected_score": projected_score,
            "projected_classification": projected_classification
        })

    forecast_model_diagnostics.append({
        "score_component": component_name,
        "ar1_intercept": intercept,
        "ar1_beta": beta,
        "residual_std": residual_std,
        "r_squared": ar1_model.rsquared
    })

forward_credit_risk_outlook = pd.DataFrame(forward_outlook_rows)

forward_credit_risk_outlook = (
    forward_credit_risk_outlook
    .round(2)
)

forecast_model_diagnostics = pd.DataFrame(
    forecast_model_diagnostics
).round(4)

forward_credit_risk_outlook

8.3.1 Forward Credit Risk Outlook with ARIMA Model SelectionÂ¶

This section creates a forward credit-risk outlook for the composite score and each category score. The purpose is to estimate whether macro-credit pressure is likely to improve, stabilize, or deteriorate over the next 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month monitoring windows.

This forecast is applied to the dashboardâ€™s own risk scores, not to S&P 500 prices. The model forecasts the composite credit-risk score and the four category scores directly:

  • Composite Credit Risk Score
  • Market / Financial Stress
  • Macro / Labor Risk
  • Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure
  • Realized Credit Performance

The main question is:

Based on the historical behavior of each risk score, what is the projected risk level over the next 1, 3, and 6 months?

A small ARIMA model-selection process is used instead of manually choosing one fixed model for every score component. ARIMA models are useful here because the score series are time-ordered, persistent, and may contain short-term autocorrelation. The model uses past score behavior to create a baseline forecast for the dashboardâ€™s own risk scores.

The ARIMA structure is written as ARIMA(p, d, q):

  • p is the autoregressive order. It controls how many prior values of the score are used.
  • d is the differencing order. It controls whether the model uses the score level or the change in the score.
  • q is the moving-average order. It controls how many prior forecast errors are used.

This project tests low-order ARIMA candidates where:

  • p = 0, 1, or 2
  • d = 0 or 1
  • q = 0, 1, or 2

Including both d = 0 and d = 1 is important. A model with d = 0 treats the score as stable enough to forecast in levels. A model with d = 1 forecasts changes in the score instead, which can be more appropriate if the score behaves like a non-stationary or drifting process. Testing both allows the data to determine whether differencing improves the model fit.

Candidate models are compared using AIC and BIC. Both are information criteria where lower values indicate a better balance between model fit and complexity.

  • AIC rewards fit but allows somewhat more model complexity.
  • BIC penalizes model complexity more strongly, especially as sample size increases.

BIC is used as the primary selection criterion because this is a monthly dashboard series with a limited number of operational observations. A simpler model is preferred unless a more complex ARIMA structure provides enough improvement to justify the additional parameters. AIC is still reported as a secondary diagnostic.

For each score component, the selected ARIMA model produces a six-month forecast path. The dashboard reports the current score, projected 1-month score, projected 3-month score, and projected 6-month score. Each projected score is then mapped back into the appropriate risk classification.

The forecast should be interpreted as a baseline monitoring outlook, not a guaranteed prediction. It does not include external future shocks such as geopolitical events, oil-price shocks, fiscal-policy changes, sudden liquidity events, or unexpected monetary-policy changes. Those variables could be added in a future SARIMAX or ARIMAX version with exogenous predictors.

import warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")


def assign_composite_regime(score):
    if pd.isna(score):
        return "Insufficient Data"
    elif score < 45:
        return "Normal"
    elif score < 55:
        return "Watch"
    elif score < 70:
        return "Elevated"
    else:
        return "Stress"


def assign_category_band(score):
    if pd.isna(score):
        return "Insufficient Data"
    elif score < 50:
        return "Normal"
    elif score < 75:
        return "Watch"
    elif score < 90:
        return "Elevated"
    else:
        return "Stress"


score_columns = {
    "Composite Credit Risk Score": "composite_credit_risk_score",
    "Market / Financial Stress": "market_financial_stress_score",
    "Macro / Labor Risk": "macro_labor_risk_score",
    "Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure": "rate_yield_curve_pressure_score",
    "Realized Credit Performance": "realized_credit_performance_score"
}


candidate_orders = []

for p in [0, 1, 2]:
    for d in [0, 1]:
        for q in [0, 1, 2]:
            candidate_orders.append((p, d, q))


model_selection_rows = []
forecast_rows = []
composite_forecast_interval_rows = []

for component_name, score_col in score_columns.items():

    series_data = (
        dashboard_score_data[["month_end", score_col]]
        .dropna()
        .copy()
        .set_index("month_end")
    )

    y = series_data[score_col].astype(float)

    best_model_fit = None
    best_order = None
    best_bic = np.inf
    best_aic = np.inf

    for order in candidate_orders:
        try:
            model = ARIMA(
                y,
                order=order,
                enforce_stationarity=False,
                enforce_invertibility=False
            )

            model_fit = model.fit()

            model_selection_rows.append({
                "score_component": component_name,
                "arima_order": str(order),
                "aic": model_fit.aic,
                "bic": model_fit.bic
            })

            if model_fit.bic < best_bic:
                best_bic = model_fit.bic
                best_aic = model_fit.aic
                best_order = order
                best_model_fit = model_fit

        except Exception:
            continue

    if best_model_fit is None:
        raise ValueError(f"No ARIMA model could be fit for {component_name}")

    forecast_result = best_model_fit.get_forecast(steps=6)
    forecast_mean = forecast_result.predicted_mean
    forecast_ci = forecast_result.conf_int()

    current_score = y.iloc[-1]

    selected_forecast_steps = {
        "Current": 0,
        "Projected 1-month": 1,
        "Projected 3-month": 3,
        "Projected 6-month": 6
    }

    for outlook_window, step in selected_forecast_steps.items():

        if step == 0:
            projected_score = current_score
            lower_range = np.nan
            upper_range = np.nan
        else:
            projected_score = forecast_mean.iloc[step - 1]
            projected_score = min(max(projected_score, 0), 100)

            lower_range = forecast_ci.iloc[step - 1, 0]
            upper_range = forecast_ci.iloc[step - 1, 1]

            lower_range = min(max(lower_range, 0), 100)
            upper_range = min(max(upper_range, 0), 100)

        if component_name == "Composite Credit Risk Score":
            projected_classification = assign_composite_regime(projected_score)
        else:
            projected_classification = assign_category_band(projected_score)

        forecast_rows.append({
            "score_component": component_name,
            "selected_arima_order": str(best_order),
            "selection_criterion": "BIC",
            "outlook_window": outlook_window,
            "projected_score": projected_score,
            "projected_classification": projected_classification
        })

        if component_name == "Composite Credit Risk Score":
            composite_forecast_interval_rows.append({
                "outlook_window": outlook_window,
                "selected_arima_order": str(best_order),
                "projected_score": projected_score,
                "lower_range": lower_range,
                "upper_range": upper_range,
                "projected_regime": projected_classification
            })


arima_model_selection_results = pd.DataFrame(model_selection_rows)

arima_selected_models = (
    arima_model_selection_results
    .sort_values(["score_component", "bic"])
    .groupby("score_component")
    .head(1)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
    .round(2)
)

forward_credit_risk_outlook = (
    pd.DataFrame(forecast_rows)
    .round(2)
)

composite_outlook_only = (
    pd.DataFrame(composite_forecast_interval_rows)
    .round(2)
)

arima_selected_models

ARIMA Model Selection ResultsÂ¶

The ARIMA model-selection process selected a separate time-series specification for each score component. This is more defensible than applying the same model structure to every score because each risk component can behave differently over time.

The selected models show that some score components are forecast in levels, while others are forecast using differenced values. The Composite Credit Risk Score and Market / Financial Stress score were selected with d = 0, meaning the models forecast the score level directly. Macro / Labor Risk, Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure, and Realized Credit Performance were selected with d = 1, meaning the models forecast changes in the score.

This distinction is useful because market stress can move quickly and mean-revert, while labor risk, rate pressure, and realized credit performance may behave more persistently. The selected model structures reflect these differences rather than forcing one forecasting structure across all score components.

The selected ARIMA models improve the forward outlook methodology compared with a simple rolling-average or momentum extrapolation. However, AIC and BIC are model-selection criteria, not full proof of forecasting accuracy. Forecast accuracy should be evaluated in a later validation step using out-of-sample forecast errors, directional accuracy, and regime-classification accuracy.

Realized Credit Performance Forecast LimitationÂ¶

The Realized Credit Performance component is based on slower-moving credit outcomes such as delinquency and charge-off indicators. These indicators are reported at lower frequency than market and rate variables and are forward-filled into the monthly dashboard framework.

Because of this lower-frequency structure, the Realized Credit Performance score can remain unchanged for several monthly observations. The selected ARIMA model projects a flat near-term path because the recent series contains very little month-to-month movement. This is not treated as a coding error, but it is treated as a forecasting limitation.

For the first version of the dashboard, the Realized Credit Performance outlook is interpreted as a conservative nowcast: the latest value is carried forward until new credit-performance data updates the category score. Future versions could improve this component by forecasting it at quarterly frequency, adding loan-level credit performance data, or incorporating forward-looking credit indicators such as lending standards, loan demand, bankruptcy filings, or credit-spread changes.

from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

diagnostic_rows = []

for _, row in arima_selected_models.iterrows():
    component_name = row["score_component"]
    selected_order = eval(row["arima_order"])

    score_col = score_columns[component_name]

    y = (
        dashboard_score_data[["month_end", score_col]]
        .dropna()
        .set_index("month_end")[score_col]
        .astype(float)
    )

    model = ARIMA(
        y,
        order=selected_order,
        enforce_stationarity=False,
        enforce_invertibility=False
    )

    model_fit = model.fit()

    residuals = model_fit.resid.dropna()

    try:
        lb_result = acorr_ljungbox(
            residuals,
            lags=[6],
            return_df=True
        )
        ljung_box_pvalue = lb_result["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0]
    except Exception:
        ljung_box_pvalue = np.nan

    try:
        adf_pvalue = adfuller(y.dropna(), autolag="AIC")[1]
    except Exception:
        adf_pvalue = np.nan

    try:
        kpss_pvalue = kpss(y.dropna(), regression="c", nlags="auto")[1]
    except Exception:
        kpss_pvalue = np.nan

    diagnostic_rows.append({
        "score_component": component_name,
        "selected_arima_order": selected_order,
        "ljung_box_pvalue_lag6": ljung_box_pvalue,
        "adf_pvalue": adf_pvalue,
        "kpss_pvalue": kpss_pvalue,
        "residual_mean": residuals.mean(),
        "residual_std": residuals.std()
    })

arima_diagnostic_summary = pd.DataFrame(diagnostic_rows).round(4)

8.3.2 ARIMA Forecast Diagnostics and Realized Credit Performance CheckÂ¶

After generating the ARIMA-based forward outlook, the Realized Credit Performance forecast remained flat at 44.29 across the 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month forecast windows. Because a completely flat forecast can indicate either a stable credit-performance series or a weak forecasting signal, an additional diagnostic check was performed.

The Realized Credit Performance score is derived from realized bank credit-performance indicators, including delinquency-rate and charge-off-rate measures. These inputs come from Federal Reserve / FRED credit-performance series such as delinquency rates and charge-off rates on loans at commercial banks. These series are reported at quarterly frequency, which makes this category slower-moving than market variables such as VIX, credit spreads, or Treasury-rate changes. [1]

The change-frequency check shows that the Realized Credit Performance score is not frozen or structurally broken. Across 259 observations, the series has 247 unique score values. Only 7 months had no score change, representing 2.70% of the sample. The average absolute monthly change is 2.27 points, and the maximum absolute monthly change is 32.45 points. This confirms that the variable changes over the full sample.

However, the most recent observations show very small monthly movements. In early 2026, Realized Credit Performance moved from 41.91 in January to 41.93 in February, 41.96 in March, 44.26 in April, 44.28 in May, and 44.29 in June. This recent pattern explains why the selected ARIMA model projects little to no short-term movement. The forecast is not saying that realized credit performance cannot change. It is saying that, based on the recent behavior of this specific score series, the model does not detect enough near-term movement to project deterioration or improvement.

This is economically reasonable because Realized Credit Performance is based on lagging credit outcomes such as delinquency and charge-off indicators. These indicators usually move more slowly than market volatility, spreads, or rate/yield-curve indicators. Because some of the underlying credit-performance inputs are lower-frequency series aligned into a monthly dashboard framework, the near-term signal can appear smoother than faster-moving market or rate variables.

The ARIMA diagnostics were reviewed to test whether the selected models are producing reasonable baseline forecasts. These diagnostics do not prove perfect forecast accuracy, but they help identify whether a model is obviously misspecified.

The Ljung-Box test checks whether the model residuals still contain autocorrelation. The null hypothesis is that residuals are not autocorrelated. A p-value above 0.05 is preferred because it suggests the model has captured most of the serial dependence in the series. For the Composite Credit Risk Score, the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.2221, which does not indicate strong remaining residual autocorrelation. Realized Credit Performance has a Ljung-Box p-value of 0.5190, which also supports the selected model from a residual-autocorrelation standpoint. Market / Financial Stress also passes this check with a p-value of 0.2938, and Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure passes at 0.1139. Macro / Labor Risk has a Ljung-Box p-value of 0.0000, which indicates remaining residual autocorrelation and means that this componentâ€™s forecast should be interpreted more cautiously.

The ADF test checks for a unit root. The null hypothesis is that the series is non-stationary. A p-value below 0.05 provides evidence against a unit root. Market / Financial Stress has an ADF p-value of 0.0036, which supports stationarity in that score series. The Composite Credit Risk Score has an ADF p-value of 0.1289, Realized Credit Performance has a p-value of 0.1826, Macro / Labor Risk has a p-value of 0.1671, and Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure has a p-value of 0.5871. These values do not strongly reject the unit-root null for those components, which is why allowing d = 1 in the ARIMA model-selection grid was important.

The KPSS test checks stationarity from the opposite direction. The null hypothesis is that the series is stationary. A p-value above 0.05 is preferred. The Composite Credit Risk Score has a KPSS p-value of 0.1000, and Market / Financial Stress also has a KPSS p-value of 0.1000, supporting stationarity under this test. Realized Credit Performance has a KPSS p-value of 0.0510, which is borderline but slightly above the 0.05 threshold. Macro / Labor Risk has a KPSS p-value of 0.0172, and Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure has a p-value of 0.0100, suggesting non-stationary or highly persistent behavior in those score series.

The ADF and KPSS tests do not always agree. When they conflict, the series may be borderline stationary, persistent, or regime-dependent. For this reason, the forecast process did not assume one fixed differencing structure for every score. The ARIMA grid allowed both d = 0 and d = 1, and the final specification was selected by BIC.

The residual mean and residual standard deviation provide additional forecast-quality context. A residual mean close to zero suggests the model is not systematically overpredicting or underpredicting. The Composite Credit Risk Score has a residual mean of -0.1852, and Realized Credit Performance has a residual mean of 0.1710, both close to zero on a 0 to 100 score scale. The residual standard deviation measures typical forecast error size. The Composite Credit Risk Score has a residual standard deviation of 4.7117 points, while Realized Credit Performance has a residual standard deviation of 5.3890 points. Macro / Labor Risk and Market / Financial Stress have larger residual standard deviations of 11.5715 and 10.0837, indicating greater uncertainty in those component forecasts.

The composite forecast remains in the Normal regime across the forecast horizon. The current Composite Credit Risk Score is 42.84. The projected score is 40.66 over 1 month, 42.17 over 3 months, and 43.56 over 6 months. However, the uncertainty range matters. The 1-month forecast range is 32.21 to 49.12, which crosses the Watch threshold of 45. The 3-month forecast range is 25.72 to 58.62, and the 6-month forecast range is 23.81 to 63.32, both of which extend into the Elevated range. This means the point forecast remains Normal, but the uncertainty bands show that the outlook is not risk-free.

Overall, the ARIMA forecast layer is a defensible baseline for Version 1 because it tests multiple model structures and selects the final specification using BIC. The diagnostics support using the Composite Credit Risk Score forecast as a baseline monitoring outlook. The Realized Credit Performance forecast is stable because the recent score history contains very little movement, not because the variable is broken. The Macro / Labor Risk forecast should be interpreted more cautiously because its residuals still show autocorrelation.

Future versions could improve this forecast layer by adding exogenous predictors such as CPI inflation, federal funds rate, oil prices, SLOOS lending standards, loan demand, bankruptcy filings, or credit-spread changes through a SARIMAX or ARIMAX framework. The Federal Reserveâ€™s Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey is especially relevant because it tracks lending standards, lending terms, and loan demand across business and household lending categories. [1]

FRED reports delinquency-rate and charge-off-rate series for commercial bank loans at quarterly frequency, and the Federal Reserveâ€™s Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey tracks lending standards, terms, and demand for bank loans.

8.4 Historical Composite Score with Forward ARIMA OutlookÂ¶

This visualization combines the historical Composite Credit Risk Score with the ARIMA-based forward outlook. The chart shows the actual historical composite score, the fitted ARIMA baseline, and the projected score path over the next six months.

This view is more useful than only plotting the forecast table because it places the forecast in historical context. It allows the dashboard to show whether the projected score is unusually high, unusually low, near a regime threshold, or consistent with recent score behavior.

The fitted ARIMA line should not be interpreted as a perfect historical prediction. It is an in-sample fitted baseline showing how the selected ARIMA model tracks the historical composite score. The forward section extends the selected model beyond the latest available month and adds a forecast range around the projected values.

The chart includes the revised composite regime thresholds:

  • Watch threshold: 45
  • Elevated threshold: 55
  • Stress threshold: 70

This helps determine whether the projected score remains inside the current regime or approaches a higher-risk regime over the forecast window.

composite_history = dashboard_score_data[

        "composite_credit_risk_score",
        "composite_credit_risk_regime_revised",

composite_history["month_end"] = pd.to_datetime(
    composite_history["month_end"]
)

composite_history = composite_history.sort_values("month_end")

# Use 2015 onward for readability.
# The ARIMA model is still trained on the full available operational composite-score history.

chart_start_date = "2015-01-01"

composite_chart_history = composite_history[
    composite_history["month_end"] >= chart_start_date
].copy()

# Refit selected composite ARIMA model on full available composite score history

selected_composite_order = eval(
    arima_selected_models.loc[
        arima_selected_models["score_component"] == "Composite Credit Risk Score",
        "arima_order"
    ].iloc[0]
)

composite_series = (
    composite_history
    .set_index("month_end")["composite_credit_risk_score"]
    .astype(float)
)

composite_arima_model = ARIMA(
    composite_series,
    order=selected_composite_order,
    enforce_stationarity=False,
    enforce_invertibility=False
)

composite_arima_fit = composite_arima_model.fit()

# In-sample fitted values

    "month_end": composite_series.index,

}).reset_index(drop=True)

# Six-month forecast

forecast_result = composite_arima_fit.get_forecast(
    steps=forecast_steps
)

forecast_mean = forecast_result.predicted_mean
forecast_ci = forecast_result.conf_int()

last_actual_date = composite_series.index[-1]

forecast_dates = pd.date_range(
    start=last_actual_date + pd.offsets.MonthEnd(1),
    periods=forecast_steps,
    freq="M"

forecast_display = pd.DataFrame({

    "forecast_score": forecast_mean.values,

})

    lower=0,
    upper=100
)

forecast_display["lower_range"] = forecast_display["lower_range"].clip(
    lower=0,
    upper=100
)

forecast_display["upper_range"] = forecast_display["upper_range"].clip(
    lower=0,
    upper=100

# Add latest actual point to connect historical line and forecast line

forecast_connector = pd.DataFrame({
    "month_end": [last_actual_date],
    "forecast_score": [composite_series.iloc[-1]],
    "lower_range": [composite_series.iloc[-1]],
    "upper_range": [composite_series.iloc[-1]]
})

forecast_display_with_connector = pd.concat(
    [
        forecast_connector,
        forecast_display

)

# Plot

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))

ax.plot(
    composite_chart_history["month_end"],
    composite_chart_history["composite_credit_risk_score"],
    label="Actual Composite Score"
)

ax.plot(
    composite_fitted_chart["month_end"],
    composite_fitted_chart["fitted_score"],
    linestyle="--",
    label="ARIMA Fitted Baseline"
)

ax.plot(
    forecast_display_with_connector["month_end"],
    forecast_display_with_connector["forecast_score"],
    marker="o",
    color="purple",
    label="ARIMA Forecast"
)

ax.fill_between(
    forecast_display_with_connector["month_end"],
    forecast_display_with_connector["lower_range"],
    forecast_display_with_connector["upper_range"],
    alpha=0.20,
    label="Forecast Range"
)

# Recession shading

for date in composite_chart_history.loc[
    composite_chart_history["usrec"] == 1,
    "month_end"
]:
    ax.axvspan(
        date,
        date + pd.offsets.MonthEnd(1),
        alpha=0.12
    )

# Revised composite thresholds
# Labels are excluded from the legend and placed directly on the chart.

watch_color = "green"
elevated_color = "goldenrod"
stress_color = "red"

ax.axhline(
    45,
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.2,
    color=watch_color,
    label="_nolegend_"
)

ax.axhline(
    55,
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.2,
    color=elevated_color,
    label="_nolegend_"
)

ax.axhline(
    70,
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.2,
    color=stress_color,
    label="_nolegend_"
)

# Place threshold labels just outside the right edge of the plot.
# x=1.01 means slightly to the right of the plotting area.
# y-values use the actual score scale.

threshold_label_x = 1.01

ax.text(
    threshold_label_x,
    45,
    "Watch Threshold (45)",
    transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
    va="center",
    ha="left",
    color=watch_color,
    clip_on=False,
    bbox=dict(facecolor="white", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="none")
)

ax.text(
    threshold_label_x,
    55,
    "Elevated Threshold (55)",
    transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
    va="center",
    ha="left",
    color=elevated_color,
    clip_on=False,
    bbox=dict(facecolor="white", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="none")
)

ax.text(
    threshold_label_x,
    70,
    "Stress Threshold (70)",
    transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
    va="center",
    ha="left",
    color=stress_color,
    clip_on=False,
    bbox=dict(facecolor="white", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="none")
)

ax.set_title("Historical Composite Credit-Risk Score with ARIMA Forecast")
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_ylabel("Composite Credit-Risk Score")
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)

# Keep only the actual/model/forecast items in the legend.
ax.legend(loc="lower left")

# Leave room on the right side for threshold labels.
plt.tight_layout()
fig.subplots_adjust(right=0.82)

plt.show()

The ARIMA model is trained on the full available operational composite-score history, while the visualization begins in 2015 for readability and to emphasize the recent forecast window.

# Convert tuple/list/object values into SQLite-safe strings before saving

def make_sqlite_safe(df):
    df_safe = df.copy()

    for col in df_safe.columns:
        df_safe[col] = df_safe[col].apply(
            lambda x: str(x) if isinstance(x, (tuple, list, dict)) else x
        )

    return df_safe
