8.5.1 Dashboard Table OutputsÂ¶

The dashboard output tables saved in Section 8 organize the final scoring, forecasting, diagnostic, and visualization-support data into reusable SQLite tables. These tables allow the notebook outputs to be reused later in a dashboard application without rerunning the full data-ingestion, feature-engineering, scoring, and model-selection pipeline.

The saved dashboard tables include the final Composite Credit Risk Score, the latest score snapshot, selected ARIMA model orders, the forward credit-risk outlook, the composite forecast range, forecast diagnostics, realized credit-performance stability checks, and chart-ready composite forecast data.

The main dashboard table is dashboard_credit_risk_score. This table contains the full operational monthly score history, including the revised composite regime, category scores, recession indicator, score coverage, and provisional-score flag.

The dashboard_current_credit_risk_snapshot table summarizes the latest dashboard reading. It is designed to support current-state interpretation by showing the latest composite score, latest category scores, prior-month scores, and recent 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month changes.

The dashboard_forward_credit_risk_outlook table stores the current, 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month forecast values for the composite score and category components. This table supports the forward-looking monitoring layer of the dashboard.

The dashboard_composite_forward_outlook_range table stores the composite score forecast range. This table is useful because the forecast range provides uncertainty context around the ARIMA point forecast.

The dashboard_arima_selected_models and dashboard_arima_diagnostic_summary tables document the selected ARIMA specifications and diagnostic checks used for the baseline forecast layer. These outputs make the forecast process more transparent and easier to audit.

The dashboard_realized_credit_change_summary table documents the recent behavior of the realized credit-performance component. This is useful because realized credit indicators such as delinquency and charge-off measures move more slowly than market and rate variables.

The dashboard_composite_forecast_chart_data table stores chart-ready data for the historical composite score and ARIMA forecast visualization.

Together, these tables separate the final dashboard outputs from the raw pipeline. This makes the project easier to extend into Streamlit because the dashboard can read from saved SQLite outputs instead of rebuilding every intermediate step.

8.6 Section 8 Wrap-UpÂ¶

Section 8 converts the scored macro-credit framework into dashboard-ready outputs.

The section begins by organizing the final Composite Credit Risk Score and revised regime labels into a clean score table. This table provides the monthly history of the dashboardâ€™s primary risk measure, along with the four underlying category scores: Market / Financial Stress, Macro / Labor Risk, Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure, and Realized Credit Performance.

The latest snapshot table then converts the historical score table into a current monitoring view. It shows the latest composite score, current regime, category-level drivers, and recent 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month changes. This helps answer whether macro-credit conditions are currently improving, stabilizing, or deteriorating.

Section 8 also creates the forward-looking baseline outlook using ARIMA model selection. Instead of forcing one model structure onto every score component, each composite or category score is evaluated using a common ARIMA candidate grid, and the selected model is chosen using information criteria. The Composite Credit Risk Score selected an ARIMA(2, 0, 2) specification, while individual category scores selected their own model orders based on their different time-series behavior.

The ARIMA forecast is used as a baseline monitoring path, not as a full stress scenario. The 1-month forecast is the most directly useful forecast window, the 3-month forecast is a reasonable monitoring baseline, and the 6-month forecast should be interpreted more cautiously because macro-credit conditions can shift quickly.

The section also documents forecast limitations. Realized Credit Performance is slower-moving because delinquency and charge-off indicators are reported at lower frequency and are forward-filled into the monthly dashboard structure. As a result, the realized credit-performance forecast may appear flat in the near term. This is treated as a limitation of the Version 1 forecast layer, not as a coding error.

The historical composite score with ARIMA forecast visualization provides the main forward-looking chart for the dashboard. It shows the recent composite score path, revised regime thresholds, baseline forecast, and forecast range.

Finally, Section 8 saves all dashboard-ready tables to SQLite. These saved outputs create the bridge between the analytical notebook and the future Streamlit dashboard. Instead of rebuilding the entire workflow each time, the dashboard can load the final score, snapshot, forecast, diagnostics, and chart-ready tables directly from the database.

The main result of Section 8 is a complete dashboard output layer: current score, current drivers, recent changes, forecast outlook, forecast diagnostics, visualization-ready data, and reusable SQLite tables.

9. VisualizationsÂ¶

Section 9 converts the dashboard-ready SQLite outputs into final visualizations. These charts are designed to communicate the current macro-credit risk score, historical regime behavior, category-level drivers, and forward ARIMA outlook.

The visualizations are built from the saved dashboard_% tables created in Section 8. This keeps the project workflow reproducible: earlier sections create and validate the scores, while this section focuses only on presenting those results clearly.

The goal of this section is to create presentation-ready charts that can be used in the final notebook, GitHub repository, and future interactive dashboard.

This section loads the saved dashboard tables from SQLite and sets the output location for saved chart files. Final chart images will be exported to the outputs/figures/ folder so they can be used in the GitHub README, portfolio materials, and later Streamlit dashboard development.

9.2 Historical Composite Credit-Risk Score with ARIMA ForecastÂ¶

This chart shows the historical Composite Credit Risk Score, the selected ARIMA fitted baseline, and the six-month forward ARIMA forecast. The visualization begins in 2015 for readability, while the selected ARIMA model was trained using the full available operational composite-score history.

The chart includes revised regime thresholds for Watch, Elevated, and Stress. The forecast line and uncertainty range show whether the projected score remains within the current regime or approaches a higher-risk threshold.

Full-History Composite Score InterpretationÂ¶

The full-history composite chart shows how the revised 45 / 55 / 70 thresholds classify macro-credit conditions across the operational sample. The revised thresholds are useful because they identify both moderate deterioration and severe broad-based stress without requiring the composite score to reach the original 90-point Stress threshold.

The 2008 credit crisis period reaches the Stress range under the revised framework, which supports the decision to use 70 as the Stress threshold. This indicates that the Stress label is reserved for severe broad-based macro-credit deterioration rather than ordinary volatility.

The 2020 recession period shows a sharp increase in the composite score, but it does not behave identically to the 2008 credit cycle. This is consistent with the interpretation that 2020 was a severe market and labor shock, while 2008 was a broader credit-system stress event.

Overall, the full-history chart supports the revised threshold framework. The composite score rises during known stress periods, separates severe credit-cycle stress from lower-risk environments, and provides a clearer historical context for interpreting the latest dashboard reading.

9.4 Latest Category Driver InterpretationÂ¶

This chart explains what is driving the current Composite Credit Risk Score by breaking the composite into its four underlying category scores:

  • Market / Financial Stress
  • Macro / Labor Risk
  • Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure
  • Realized Credit Performance

Each category score is a percentile-based risk score from 0 to 100, where higher values indicate greater historical risk pressure in that part of the macro-credit environment. These are not raw data values and they are not regression coefficients. Instead, they are constructed through the projectâ€™s scoring framework:

  1. Raw macro-credit indicators are collected from public sources.
  2. Daily, monthly, and quarterly series are aligned into a monthly dashboard structure.
  3. Features are engineered using levels, moving averages, and point-to-point changes.
  4. Each feature is directionally transformed so that higher values consistently represent higher risk.
  5. Each feature is converted into an expanding percentile score to avoid lookahead bias.
  6. Related feature percentile scores are averaged into category scores.
  7. The four category scores are then averaged into the Composite Credit Risk Score.

This percentile-based approach makes indicators with different units comparable. For example, VIX, unemployment, Treasury yields, credit spreads, delinquency rates, and charge-off rates all have different scales, so converting them into percentile risk scores places them onto a common 0â€“100 framework.

The four category drivers represent different channels of macro-credit stress:

  • Market / Financial Stress captures fast-moving financial stress through indicators such as VIX, corporate credit spread pressure, and the St. Louis Fed Financial Stress Index.
  • Macro / Labor Risk captures labor-market deterioration, primarily through unemployment-related features, which matter because weakening employment can eventually pressure borrower repayment capacity.
  • Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure captures interest-rate pressure and yield-curve stress, including the transformed inversion-risk signal.
  • Realized Credit Performance captures observed credit deterioration through delinquency and charge-off indicators. These are the most direct credit-performance measures, but they tend to move more slowly than market variables because they are more lagging in nature.

This chart is designed to identify the current risk drivers, not to assign final regimes to each category. The final dashboard regime is based on the Composite Credit Risk Score, which is the equal-weighted average of the four category scores.

The vertical dashed reference line shows the current Composite Credit Risk Score. Category scores above the composite line are contributing more heavily to the current reading, while category scores below the composite line are contributing less.

The â€œ1M Î”â€ label next to each bar shows the one-month point-to-point change in that category score. A positive value means that categoryâ€™s risk pressure increased over the prior month, while a negative value means that risk pressure declined.

In the latest reading, Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure is the largest category driver, while Market / Financial Stress and Macro / Labor Risk are lower contributors. This indicates that the current composite score is not being driven by broad-based stress across all categories. Instead, the primary pressure is concentrated in the rate/yield-curve component.

9.5 Category Risk Scores Over TimeÂ¶

This chart shows the historical movement of the four category-level risk scores that make up the Composite Credit Risk Score. Each category is measured on the same 0 to 100 percentile-risk scale, where higher values indicate greater historical risk pressure.

The purpose of this visualization is to show that the four risk categories do not always move together. Market stress can move quickly, labor risk can lag, rate/yield-curve pressure can appear before realized credit deterioration, and realized credit performance can move more slowly as delinquencies and charge-offs materialize.

This chart helps explain why the composite score is useful: it summarizes broad macro-credit stress while still allowing the dashboard to identify which category is driving the score during different periods.

Category Risk Score Trend InterpretationÂ¶

The category score trend chart shows that the four components of the composite score behave differently across the credit cycle. This supports the decision to keep category-level scores visible instead of relying only on the final composite score.

Market / Financial Stress tends to move quickly during periods of market volatility, liquidity stress, and credit-spread pressure. This category is useful for identifying faster-moving stress signals because market prices and volatility indicators can adjust quickly when investors reprice risk.

Macro / Labor Risk tends to rise during or after economic deterioration because labor-market stress often develops after financial conditions have already weakened. In this dashboard, labor risk is therefore more useful as a confirmation and persistence signal than as the earliest warning signal.

Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure can behave differently from the other categories because rate pressure and yield-curve inversion may appear before realized credit losses. A higher score in this category means the rate/yield-curve channel is contributing more macro-credit risk relative to its own historical distribution. This can happen before recession conditions are fully visible in labor or credit-performance data.

Realized Credit Performance tends to move more slowly because delinquency and charge-off indicators are observed credit outcomes. These indicators confirm that credit deterioration has reached borrowers and bank loan performance, but they may lag faster-moving market, rate, and labor signals.

This chart helps explain why the composite score can remain moderate even when one category is elevated. A high score in one category does not automatically mean broad-based credit stress. The dashboard becomes more concerning when multiple categories rise together.

Source note: The interpretation of yield-curve pressure as an early macro-risk signal is consistent with Federal Reserve research describing the Treasury yield curve slope and inversion as leading recession indicators. The interpretation of realized credit performance as a slower-moving confirmation channel is based on the Federal Reserveâ€™s charge-off and delinquency rate data, where delinquency and charge-off measures represent observed credit-performance outcomes rather than forward-looking market prices.

Trailing 12-Month Category Score InterpretationÂ¶

The trailing 12-month chart provides a closer view of the recent movement in the four category scores and the composite score. This chart is useful because the full-history view can hide recent month-to-month changes.

A downward movement in a category score means risk pressure has eased in that category according to the dashboardâ€™s percentile framework. An upward movement means that risk pressure has increased.

In the latest period, the dashboard should be interpreted by comparing both the level and direction of each category. A high category score indicates that the category remains an important risk driver, while a negative recent change indicates that the category has eased from its prior level.

This distinction is important for Macro / Labor Risk. A falling labor-risk score means the dashboardâ€™s labor-risk inputs are lower than they were in prior months, not necessarily that every current labor-market release is strong. Newer labor-market deterioration may appear first in the weekly credit-risk brief before it is fully reflected in the dashboardâ€™s monthly scoring inputs.

9.6 Composite Regime DistributionÂ¶

This chart shows the distribution of monthly Composite Credit Risk Score regimes under the revised threshold framework.

The revised composite regimes are:

  • Normal: below 45
  • Watch: 45 to below 55
  • Elevated: 55 to below 70
  • Stress: 70 and above

The purpose of this visualization is to show whether the revised thresholds produce a practical regime distribution. A useful regime framework should classify most months as Normal or Watch, while reserving Elevated and Stress for more severe historical periods.

InÂ [84]:
composite_regime_distribution = (
    dashboard_credit_risk_score
    .groupby("composite_credit_risk_regime_revised")
    .agg(
        month_count=("month_end", "count"),
        recession_months=("usrec", "sum"),
        avg_composite_score=("composite_credit_risk_score", "mean")
    )
    .reset_index()
)

composite_regime_distribution["month_share_pct"] = (
    100
    * composite_regime_distribution["month_count"]
    / composite_regime_distribution["month_count"].sum()
)

composite_regime_distribution["recession_share_pct"] = (
    100
    * composite_regime_distribution["recession_months"]
    / composite_regime_distribution["month_count"]
)

regime_order = ["Normal", "Watch", "Elevated", "Stress"]

composite_regime_distribution["regime_order"] = (
    composite_regime_distribution["composite_credit_risk_regime_revised"]
    .map({regime: i for i, regime in enumerate(regime_order)})
)

composite_regime_distribution = (
    composite_regime_distribution
    .sort_values("regime_order")
    .drop(columns="regime_order")
    .round(2)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

Composite Regime Distribution InterpretationÂ¶

The composite regime distribution shows how often the dashboard classified monthly macro-credit conditions as Normal, Watch, Elevated, or Stress.

9.8 Section 9 Wrap-UpÂ¶

Section 9 converts the dashboard-ready score outputs into final visualization files. The visualizations summarize the historical Composite Credit Risk Score, the ARIMA-based forward outlook, category-level risk drivers, category score trends, and revised regime distribution.

The visualizations serve three purposes:

  1. Current monitoring: identify the latest composite score, current regime, and main category drivers.
  2. Historical validation: show how the score and revised thresholds behaved across prior recession and stress periods.
  3. Forward outlook: display the ARIMA-based six-month composite score forecast and uncertainty range.

These charts are saved as .png files in the outputs/figures/ folder and are ready to be used in the GitHub README, business interpretation section, and future interactive dashboard.

10. Business InterpretationÂ¶

Section 10 translates the final dashboard outputs into business-facing interpretation. The goal is to explain what the current macro-credit risk score means, what is driving the score, how the current reading compares with historical stress regimes, and how the forward ARIMA outlook should be interpreted.

This section uses the final dashboard tables and visualizations created in Sections 8 and 9 to answer the main project question:

Are macro-credit conditions deteriorating, and do those regimes provide context for recession risk and market behavior?

The interpretation is structured around four questions:

  1. What is the current Composite Credit Risk Score and regime?
  2. Which category is driving the current score?
  3. Does the current reading suggest broad-based stress or concentrated risk?
  4. What does the forward outlook imply over the next 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month monitoring windows?

Realized Credit Performance remained nearly unchanged, with a latest score of 44.31 and a 1-month change of only +0.02.

Overall, the latest reading suggests concentrated risk rather than broad-based macro-credit stress. The main current pressure is Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure. Market stress increased over the prior month, but Macro / Labor Risk declined enough to keep the overall composite score in the Normal regime.

10.3 Forward Outlook Business InterpretationÂ¶

The forward outlook uses the ARIMA forecast created earlier in the notebook to project the Composite Credit Risk Score over the next 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month monitoring windows.

This section does not introduce a new model. It interprets the forecast output already created in Section 8.3.

The purpose is to answer a simple business question:

Is the dashboardâ€™s composite credit-risk score expected to improve, remain stable, or deteriorate over the near-term monitoring window?

The point forecast shows the modelâ€™s baseline projection for the Composite Credit Risk Score. The forecast range shows the uncertainty around that projection.

A current score below 45 is classified as Normal. A projected score that remains below 45 suggests the baseline outlook remains contained. If the upper forecast range crosses above 45 or 55, that means the baseline outlook is still contained, but there is some upside risk toward Watch or Elevated conditions.

ARIMA Model Selection NoteÂ¶

The composite score and the individual category scores were forecasted separately. Each score series was tested across the same ARIMA candidate grid, and the final order was selected using BIC.

The Composite Credit Risk Score selected an ARIMA(2, 0, 2) model. This means the model uses two autoregressive terms, no differencing, and two moving-average terms.

The individual category forecasts use different ARIMA orders because each category has different time-series behavior. Market / Financial Stress can move quickly, Macro / Labor Risk can lag, Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure can remain persistent, and Realized Credit Performance tends to move more slowly.

Because of this, the category forecasts should be interpreted as separate component outlooks, not as manually summed forecasts. The main dashboard forecast is the Composite Credit Risk Score forecast, while the category forecasts help explain which underlying risk channels are expected to rise, fall, or remain stable.

Forward Outlook SummaryÂ¶

The latest observed Composite Credit Risk Score is 43.14, which places the dashboard in the Normal regime.

The ARIMA forecast projects the composite score to move to approximately:

  • 44.30 over the next 1 month
  • 44.83 over the next 3 months
  • 45.21 over the next 6 months

Based on the point forecast, the composite score remains in the Normal regime over the 1-month and 3-month windows, but moves into the Watch regime by the 6-month window.

The forecast range is still important. The upper forecast range reaches approximately 64.92, which falls in the Elevated range. This means the baseline forecast shows only mild deterioration, but the uncertainty range allows for a higher-risk outcome if conditions weaken.

Overall, the forward outlook suggests that macro-credit risk is mildly deteriorating but still contained. The dashboard does not currently project broad-based Stress conditions, but the 6-month forecast moving into Watch means the score should be monitored closely for continued deterioration.

Component Forecast InterpretationÂ¶

The component forecast table shows how the four category scores are projected to move over the same forecast window.

The main projected pressure remains Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure. Its score is currently 74.94 and is projected to remain high at 69.08 over the 6-month window. Even though this category is projected to ease slightly, it remains the largest contributor to the composite score.

Market / Financial Stress is projected to rise from 27.54 currently to 46.10 over the 6-month window. This is still below the category Watch threshold of 50, but it shows that market stress is projected to increase from a low level.

Macro / Labor Risk is projected to rise from 25.75 to 34.12, but it remains in the Normal range. This means the model does not yet project severe labor-risk pressure based on the dashboardâ€™s current monthly inputs.

Realized Credit Performance remains stable at 44.31 across the forecast window. This reflects the slower-moving nature of delinquency and charge-off indicators.

The component forecast supports the composite forecast. The dashboard is not projecting broad-based stress across all four categories. Instead, the main current and projected pressure remains concentrated in the rate/yield-curve channel, with some projected increase in market/financial stress.

10.4 Main Business Questions AnsweredÂ¶

The dashboard was built to answer whether macro-credit conditions are deteriorating and whether those conditions provide useful context for recession risk, market behavior, and near-term monitoring.

Based on the latest dashboard output, the current Composite Credit Risk Score is 43.14, which remains in the Normal regime. This is below the revised Watch threshold of 45, so the dashboard does not currently indicate broad-based macro-credit stress.

The Composite Credit Risk Score is measured on a 0-to-100 risk scale, where higher values indicate greater macro-credit pressure. The score is calculated as an equal-weighted average of four category scores: Market / Financial Stress, Macro / Labor Risk, Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure, and Realized Credit Performance. Each category receives a 25% weight in the final composite score.

The equal 25% category weighting is a Version 1 design choice. It is used for transparency and interpretability rather than because the notebook proves that each category has the same predictive importance. Equal weighting prevents the first version from overfitting category weights to a limited historical sample or assigning arbitrary importance to one risk channel before formal validation. Lookahead bias is handled separately through the expanding-percentile scoring framework, not through the equal-weight choice.

Because all category inputs are transformed so that higher values consistently represent greater risk, each category contributes in the same risk direction. However, the categories can still offset one another because they capture different parts of the credit cycle. Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure may rise before recession conditions are visible, while Macro / Labor Risk and Realized Credit Performance may confirm deterioration later.

The category scores are also measured on a 0-to-100 category risk-score scale. Therefore, when a category increases by 9.98 points, that means the categoryâ€™s risk score increased by 9.98 points on its own 0-to-100 scale. Because each category receives a 25% weight, that 9.98-point category increase contributes approximately 2.50 points to the composite score, all else equal.

The current reading is close to Watch. The dashboard shows that risk is concentrated in one major channel: Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure. This category has the highest current score at 74.94, meaning interest-rate and yield-curve pressure remain the main source of macro-credit risk.

The current risk picture is concentrated rather than broad-based. Broad-based risk would mean that multiple categories are elevated at the same time across market stress, labor risk, rate/yield-curve pressure, and realized credit performance. In the latest reading, the main pressure is concentrated in Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure, while the other categories do not currently confirm broad stress across the full dashboard.

The recent change pattern is mixed. The Composite Credit Risk Score increased by 0.30 points over the prior month, which indicates slight deterioration. However, the score is still down 9.78 points over the prior three months and down 1.71 points over the prior six months. This means the latest month showed renewed pressure, but the broader recent trend remains more contained than earlier in the year.

The category-level changes explain why the composite score stayed in the Normal regime. Market / Financial Stress increased by 9.98 category-score points over the prior month, contributing approximately +2.50 composite-score points after applying the 25% category weight. Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure increased by 2.82 category-score points, contributing approximately +0.71 composite-score points. These movements pushed the composite score higher.

However, Macro / Labor Risk declined by 11.64 category-score points, contributing approximately -2.91 composite-score points and offsetting much of the deterioration from market stress and rate/yield-curve pressure. Realized Credit Performance was nearly unchanged, with only a 0.02 category-score point increase. This explains why the total composite score increased only 0.30 points even though some individual categories moved more sharply.

The trailing 12-month category chart shows that the current reading is contained but not flat. Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure remains the highest category score, while Market / Financial Stress and Macro / Labor Risk have moved more sharply month to month. Realized Credit Performance is more stable, which is expected because delinquency and charge-off measures tend to move more slowly.

The historical validation supports the use of the revised regime framework. The score and category components behaved sensibly around major stress periods. Market / Financial Stress reacted quickly during stress episodes, Macro / Labor Risk and Realized Credit Performance tended to confirm deterioration later, and Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure behaved more like an early-warning or policy-pressure channel. The revised thresholds created more useful separation than the original thresholds because Normal months were largely associated with ordinary conditions, while Elevated and Stress regimes were more closely associated with recession or broad macro-credit deterioration.

The forward outlook shows mild deterioration. The Composite Credit Risk Score is projected to rise from 43.14 currently to 44.30 over 1 month, 44.83 over 3 months, and 45.21 over 6 months. The 6-month projection crosses into the Watch regime.

The ARIMA forecast should be read as a baseline monitoring path, not as a stress scenario. The point forecast shows mild movement toward Watch, while the forecast range shows that a higher-risk path is possible if conditions weaken.

The forecast should also be interpreted with its uncertainty range and diagnostics in mind. The ARIMA layer provides a transparent baseline outlook, but it does not replace rolling-origin forecast validation, scenario analysis, or broader macro-policy inputs. The 1-month outlook is the most directly useful monitoring window, the 3-month outlook is a reasonable baseline, and the 6-month outlook should be interpreted more cautiously.

The 6-month forecast should be treated cautiously because macro-credit conditions can change quickly when new market, labor, policy, inflation, or credit information arrives. ARIMA projects the score based on the historical behavior of the score itself. If conditions remain broadly similar, the forecast provides a useful baseline trend. However, if new shocks occur, the actual score can move faster than the smoothed 6-month baseline path.

S&P 500 Market-Context QuestionÂ¶

The dashboard also tested whether revised macro-credit regimes and regime transitions provided useful context for future S&P 500 returns.

The S&P 500 results should be interpreted as market-context validation, not as a trading model or standalone equity-return forecast. The S&P 500 variables were not used to construct the Composite Credit Risk Score. They were retained as forward-looking outcome variables to test whether macro-credit regimes were associated with different future equity-market outcomes.

The regime-level S&P 500 validation did not support a simple rule that higher macro-credit risk automatically leads to weaker future S&P 500 returns. In the available S&P 500 window, Normal months had average forward S&P 500 returns of approximately 0.68% over 1 month, 2.32% over 3 months, and 5.20% over 6 months. Watch months had average forward returns of approximately 1.13%, 3.23%, and 7.23% over the same horizons. Elevated months had stronger average forward returns of approximately 4.49% over 1 month, 11.83% over 3 months, and 17.95% over 6 months.

This result means the S&P 500 relationship is timing-dependent. Higher macro-credit risk did not automatically imply weaker future equity returns in this sample. One explanation is that by the time the dashboard reaches an Elevated regime, some bad news may already be priced into equity markets, allowing forward returns to improve if conditions stabilize, policy support becomes more visible, or risk appetite recovers.

The transition-level validation added a second market-context check. The most useful transition signal was Normal â†’ Watch. This transition had the worst observed 3-month forward S&P 500 downside at approximately -16.45%, along with negative-return shares of 40.0% over 1 month, 20.0% over 3 months, and 30.0% over 6 months. This suggests that the first move out of Normal conditions may be the clearest early-warning transition in the current framework.

However, the transition evidence was limited. The Watch â†’ Elevated transition occurred only 4 times in the available S&P 500 window, and its average forward returns were strongly positive: approximately 4.37% over 1 month, 12.02% over 3 months, and 16.21% over 6 months. The worst observed 3-month forward return after Watch â†’ Elevated was still positive at approximately 9.66%. This reinforces that the relationship is not mechanically bearish and should not be treated as a reliable S&P 500 forecasting rule.

The conclusion is that the S&P 500 overlay adds useful market context, but it does not provide enough evidence for standalone financial decision-making. The dashboard can help frame risk-on / risk-off discussion and portfolio-monitoring context, but it should not be used as a mechanical S&P 500 forecasting or trading signal.

A stronger future version could test this question more formally by using longer market-history data, alternative regime thresholds, additional transition definitions, rolling validation, volatility measures, rate-shock variables, and broader macro-policy inputs. In Version 1, the number of regime transitions is too limited to support a conclusive transition-based equity forecasting strategy.

The main business conclusion is that current macro-credit risk is contained but close to Watch. The dashboard does not show broad-based stress across all four categories, but Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure remains elevated, Market / Financial Stress has recently increased, and the forecast suggests continued monitoring is warranted.

10.5 Limitations and Version 2 EnhancementsÂ¶

This dashboard evaluates aggregate credit conditions using public macroeconomic, market, rate, and credit-performance indicators.

The ARIMA forecast should be interpreted as a baseline score projection. The model forecasts the dashboard score based on the scoreâ€™s own historical behavior. This makes the forecast useful for monitoring direction, but it should not be treated as a complete stress scenario.

The 1-month forecast is the most directly useful forecast window. The 3-month forecast is a reasonable monitoring baseline. The 6-month forecast should be interpreted more cautiously because macro-credit conditions can shift materially over that time frame.

The forecast range reflects model-based statistical uncertainty around the ARIMA baseline. It may capture ordinary historical score volatility, but it does not explicitly model future geopolitical shocks, energy-price shocks, Federal Reserve surprises, sudden labor-market deterioration, or liquidity events. Because of this, the forecast range should be used as a monitoring band rather than as guaranteed accuracy.

The project has not yet completed rolling-origin forecast validation. As a result, the notebook does not formally prove whether the 1-month, 3-month, or 6-month horizon is most accurate. Based on the recent volatility of the score, the 6-month point forecast should be treated as a directional monitoring path rather than a precise estimate.

The Version 1 labor category is intentionally simple. Macro / Labor Risk is primarily based on unemployment-related monthly features. It does not yet include payroll growth, initial jobless claims, continuing claims, JOLTS openings, labor-force participation, wage growth, or payroll revisions. Because of this, newer labor-market weakness may appear in a weekly macro brief before it is fully reflected in the dashboard score.

Inflation is not directly scored as its own input category in Version 1. The project includes nominal interest-rate and yield-curve pressure, but it does not separately score CPI, core CPI, inflation expectations, wage inflation, or real interest rates.

This distinction matters because nominal interest rates do not fully describe monetary pressure. The same nominal rate can imply different levels of restrictiveness depending on inflation. For example, a 5% Fed Funds rate is much tighter when inflation is 2% than when inflation is 6%.

Real rates would help address this limitation. A real interest rate adjusts a nominal interest rate for inflation. For example, if the nominal 10-year Treasury yield is 4.5% and expected inflation is 2.5%, the approximate real 10-year rate is 2.0%. Version 2 could use real rates to better measure whether monetary conditions are restrictive after inflation is considered.

Version 1 also uses equal category weights for transparency and interpretability. Each of the four categories receives a 25% weight in the Composite Credit Risk Score. This makes the score easy to explain, but it assumes that Market / Financial Stress, Macro / Labor Risk, Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure, and Realized Credit Performance contribute equally to aggregate macro-credit risk.

The S&P 500 market-context overlay is also limited by sample size. Because the FRED S&P 500 series begins later than the full credit-risk dataset, the forward-return and transition checks have fewer observations than the recession-validation tests. Future versions could expand the market-context layer by testing alternative regime thresholds, adding longer market-history sources, evaluating additional equity and credit-market outcomes, and using rolling validation to test whether regime transitions provide stable forward-looking information.

Version 2 could test alternative weighting schemes using historical validation against recession periods, credit-spread widening, realized credit deterioration, and market downside. This would make the composite score more empirically calibrated rather than purely equal-weighted.

Version 2 should also include feature-level driver analysis. The current dashboard explains which category is driving the composite score. Feature-level analysis would go one layer deeper and explain which specific indicators are driving each category.

For example, Market / Financial Stress is built from inputs such as VIX, corporate credit-spread pressure, and STLFSI4. STLFSI4 is the St. Louis Fed Financial Stress Index, which summarizes broad financial stress conditions across multiple market indicators. A feature-level table would show whether Market / Financial Stress increased because of VIX, credit spreads, STLFSI4, or their recent changes.

The strongest Version 2 enhancements would be:

  • Add broader labor-market indicators.
  • Add inflation, real-rate, and inflation-expectation indicators.
  • Add lending-standard and credit-supply indicators.
  • Compare 1-month and 3-month forecast horizons more directly, with less emphasis on the 6-month point forecast.
  • Add rolling-origin forecast validation.
  • Add scenario analysis for macro shocks.
  • Add feature-level driver decomposition.
  • Test alternative category-weighting schemes.

10.6 Section10 Wrap-UpÂ¶

Section 10 converts the dashboard outputs into a business-facing interpretation.

The latest Composite Credit Risk Score remains in the Normal regime at 43.14, but the score is close to the revised Watch threshold of 45. The current risk picture is concentrated rather than broad-based. Rate / Yield-Curve Pressure remains the largest driver, while Market / Financial Stress increased over the prior month and Macro / Labor Risk declined enough to offset part of that deterioration.

The ARIMA forecast projects mild deterioration, with the composite score moving from 43.14 currently to 45.21 over the 6-month window. This crosses into the Watch regime, but the forecast should be treated as a baseline monitoring path rather than a stress scenario.

The S&P 500 market-context validation adds an additional interpretation layer: regime transitions, especially Normal â†’ Watch, may help frame market-risk discussion, but the evidence is exploratory and not strong enough to support standalone equity-market forecasting decisions.

The final interpretation is that macro-credit risk is currently contained but close to Watch. The dashboard should continue monitoring whether pressure spreads from rate/yield-curve conditions into market stress, labor deterioration, and realized credit performance.
